desc:
The longest common subsequence of two strings is often not unique: several different strings can have the maximum length. Count how many distinct strings (as texts, not as position choices) are common subsequences of s and t with the maximum possible length.

Return the count modulo 1,000,000,007. If the strings have no common character the only longest common subsequence is the empty string, so the answer is 1.

s = "acac", t = "caca"  ->  2   ("aca" and "cac")
s = "aaa",  t = "aa"    ->  1   ("aa")
s = "ac",   t = "ca"    ->  2   ("a" and "c")
constraints: Both strings contain only the letters a, c, g and t
hints: First compute the usual LCS length table on suffixes: L[i][j] is the LCS length of s[i:] and t[j:]. Counting position choices would count the same text many times, so count texts instead.

Group the longest common subsequences by their first letter c. For a fixed c, the string c + w is a common subsequence exactly when w is a common subsequence of what follows the first occurrence of c in s[i:] and the first occurrence of c in t[j:].

Let g(i, j) be the number of distinct LCS strings of the suffixes. For every letter c with first occurrences p in s[i:] and q in t[j:], add g(p+1, q+1) if L[p+1][q+1] == L[i][j] - 1. With L[i][j] == 0, g = 1 (only the empty string).
editorial: Let L[i][j] be the LCS length for the suffixes s[i:] and t[j:], and g[i][j] the number of distinct strings of length L[i][j] that are common subsequences of those suffixes. If L[i][j] = 0, only the empty string qualifies, so g = 1.

Otherwise classify the strings by their first letter c. A string c + w is a subsequence of s[i:] iff w is a subsequence of the part of s after the first occurrence of c (greedy earliest matching is always at least as good), and the same holds for t. So for each letter c let p be its first position at or after i in s and q its first position at or after j in t (skip the letter if either does not exist). The strings starting with c that have maximum length correspond to maximum-length strings w for the pair (p+1, q+1), but only if that pair can reach length L[i][j] - 1, i.e. L[p+1][q+1] == L[i][j] - 1. Then add g[p+1][q+1]. Different first letters give different strings, and different w give different strings, so nothing is counted twice.

The answer is g[0][0] mod 1,000,000,007. Precompute the next-occurrence index of each letter for s and t, which makes each cell cost O(sigma) with sigma = 4. The total time is O(sigma · m · n). A brute-force approach that enumerates all common subsequences is exponential, and counting position choices (as in the matching-pairs problem) would count one text many times.
